newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro shares gain, dollar slips from yen high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro shares gain, dollar slips from yen high.

text.p: European shares took heart on Monday from a rebound on Wall Street and advanced despite nagging doubts over interest rates and the U.S. market's outlook.
"We've had a predictable mark-up this morning but it's anyone's guess if it will last," the head of sales and trading at a large London investment bank said.
"A lot of people are still worried about the threat of higher interest rates."

The dollar, meanwhile, was knocked off its strongest level against then yen since March 1993 after Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa said Japan would "continue to deal appropriately" with extreme currency market movements.
Excessive weakness or strength in the yen were not good for the Japanese economy, he said.

The dollar, which flirted with 117 yen in Asian trading, had settled at around 116.50 in the ensuing European business before slipping back to a low of 115.65 after Ogawa's comments -- below late rates last week.
"People are getting a bit wary on dollar/yen. They're thinking that at these sorts of levels the Japanese authorities don't want the yen to weaken too much more," said one British bank trader.
But analysts said negative perceptions of the Japanese economy and low interest rates there still prompted concern over an outflow of funds and should continue to bolster the dollar.
Tokyo markets made a shaky start to the new year on Monday as the yen slid to its lowest level against the dollar in almost four years, dragging stocks and bonds down in its wake.
The 225-share Nikkei average fell by as much as 150 points before reviving to close at 19,446.00, up 84.65 points.
Against the mark, the U.S. currency slipped from a high in Asian trading of 1.5714 but, at around 1.5660 marks, it was still up from Friday's late European levels.
"I think negative factors in Japan and Germany will remain the overriding factors continuing to weigh down both the yen and the mark," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.
On the London stock market, Europe's busiest, shares started firmer after Wall Street's surge on Friday but fear of higher interest rates was preying on market sentiment, dealers said.
The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 101.60 points to 6,544.09, almost recovering all its losses earlier last week.
New York analysts said the sharp turnaround suggested investors had shaken off the impact of strong economic indicators -- possible omens of higher interest rates -- on the bond market.
This week the main focus for markets seeking to gauge the temperature of the world's biggest economy will be U.S. jobs figures on Friday.
If non-farm payroll statistics turn out to be stronger than forecast, jitters over higher rates could send markets lower on both sides of the Atlantic, dealers said.
"The Dow is due for some sort of correction. A jump in the U.S. non-farm payroll total could be the trigger for the start of a sell-off," one London dealer said.
In Frankfurt, shares opened firmer, aided by the stronger dollar -- good news for German exporters -- and the rebound in New York.

French shares also began the week with a jump of just over one percent, buoyed by Wall Street's gains and the dollar's performance against European currencies. Traders tipped more active trading after the seasonal holiday lull.
CURRENCIES AT 1030 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.5660 marks and 115.85 yen, compared with 1.5580 and 116.33 in late business on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1030 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares was up 15.2 points to 4,104.7.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt was 32.86 higher at 2,892.14. In Paris, the CAC-40 share index gained 23.45 to 2,306.21.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold remained weak and dipped to its lowest in over three years. It was quoted around $359.50 an ounce, down from Friday's London close of $362.15. Silver slipped two cents to $4.67.
